questions.problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the $x$-axis, for $\pi \le x\le 2\pi .$ Express ${\int }_{C}xdx-(x-y)dy$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14227492/assets/264cb888010525848f647669653d34383535dd32e6ac264927105540c3b85f9f.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=-(x-y).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):\pi \le x\le 2\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying the Green's Theorem we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xdx-(x-y)dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}^{0}dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡y,{x}^{2}-2y⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the square $0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi ,$ traversed counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14227492/assets/4f75ee554c61dc799273c2c731d608766d27987937d0058df6ee1e0290d8b060.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi \}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{[2xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi }\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\pi x+2)\,dx \\  & ={[\pi {x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & ={\pi }^{3}+2\pi  \\  & =\pi ({\pi }^{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{3}+2{y}^{2},{x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,0)$ and $(1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14227492/assets/73bf9b973e50c540a873f4f1a44d936474e4c49d7041a330902508a840645009.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{3}+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):y\le x\le 2-y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{3}+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}-4xy]}_{y}^{2-y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(2-y)^{2}-4(2-y)y-{y}^{2}+4{y}^{2}]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8{y}^{2}-12y+4)\,dy \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-3y+1)\,dy \\  & =4{[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}+y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{3}{2}+1] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,2)$ and $(-2,2),$ traversed counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14227492/assets/7ca4b6fe3a5a16c4004c75b0e4524cc3b42550cb2413d5b8e1c21a1d53cee902.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3})dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{8{y}^{3}}{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{[{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot {2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=x+2.$ Express ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$  where $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+x)-{y}^{2},{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}⟩,$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14227492/assets/e32b8e7d6ce80d7cedad928f9a2f7acc3c3d7f06add7909e856db27d154068d6.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+x)-{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+x)-{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x+2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x+2}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
